text: The advent of precise germline editing has reignited a debate once confined to dystopian fiction. Advocates emphasize the therapeutic efficacy of correcting heritable disease before it manifests, framing the technology as an altruistic extension of medicine's mandate to relieve suffering, whether curative or merely palliative. Yet the proliferation of such techniques raises questions that informed consent cannot resolve: a future child cannot consent to alterations made before birth, and their autonomy is thus circumvented by decisions taken on their behalf. Critics discern in this an echo of eugenics, though defenders retort that correcting a single-gene disorder is categorically distinct from selecting for intelligence or temperament. This is, in essence, a slippery-slope argument, and like most such arguments it is neither self-evidently true nor easily dismissed; a narrow, stringent exception can be exacerbated by commercial pressure into a broader, less equitable practice. Absent a coordinated moratorium, or a rigorously enforced regulatory framework, the risk is not that germline editing proves inefficacious, but that its promise becomes commodified, available chiefly to those who can already afford every advantage.

questions.question: What is the author's primary concern about germline editing, as expressed in the passage?
options: That it is technically infeasible
That unequal access could make the technology available mainly to the already privileged
That it will inevitably lead to eugenics with no possible distinction
That scientists have not developed informed consent forms

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the 'slippery slope' argument against germline editing can best be described as
options: Dismissive, regarding it as fundamentally flawed
Fully accepting, treating it as certain to occur
Cautiously acknowledging, neither endorsing nor rejecting it outright
Enthusiastically endorsing it as a decisive objection

questions.question: Why does the author say a future child's autonomy is 'circumvented'?
options: Because the child will grow up without legal rights
Because germline modifications are made before the child can consent to them
Because parents are legally barred from giving consent
Because autonomy does not apply to unborn children under any framework

options: They deny that eugenics ever historically existed
They argue that treating single-gene disorders differs categorically from selecting for traits like intelligence
They agree the comparison is entirely apt
They claim historical eugenics programs were beneficial

Palliative approaches are always more effective than curative ones
The two terms are used interchangeably with no distinction
Palliative care is portrayed as unethical in the passage

questions.question: The passage's concluding sentence primarily warns against

Unequal commercial access undermining the equitable promise of the technology
Complete prohibition of all genetic research
The abandonment of any regulatory framework whatsoever
